findings.title: Global group view permission is treated as permission to manage groups
findings.body: `canManage()` evaluates both `view` and `manage` scopes on the all-groups resource. Consequently, an administrator granted only the Groups `view` scope passes `GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup()`, which relies on `requireManage()`, and can create groups despite having no manage permission. `canManage()` must require only the `manage` scope; `view` should remain sufficient only for view/list operations.

findings.title: User search is filtered with authorization resource IDs instead of group IDs
findings.body: `getGroupIdsWithViewPermission()` adds `groupResource.getId()`, which is the generated authorization Resource ID, not the Keycloak group ID. Callers put this set into `UserModel.GROUPS` and pass it to user search/count providers, which expect actual group IDs. As a result, an admin granted `view-members` or `manage-members` on a group cannot discover that group's users through list/search/count endpoints (despite direct per-user authorization succeeding). Add the resource name, which is created from the group ID, rather than the authorization resource ID.

findings.title: Existing admin-permissions clients are never updated with the new Groups schema
findings.body: `init()` returns immediately whenever the realm already has an admin-permissions client. Realms that enabled fine-grained authorization before this change therefore retain a resource server with no Groups resource, no Groups scopes, and no corresponding schema resource. Creating a Groups scope permission subsequently fails because `getOrCreateResource()` cannot find the new scopes, while permission evaluation can dereference a missing all-groups resource. Initialization needs to reconcile/add newly introduced schema scopes and resource-type resources for existing clients, or an explicit database migration must do so.
